# RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews the literature on which the study builds and identifies the gaps that the research questions address. It begins with NLP of disaster posts and the lack of annotated resources for Taglish. It then covers multi-task learning, negative transfer, and multi-task optimizers. It ends with a taxonomy matrix that compares the key studies and a synthesis of the literature.

## Natural Language Processing of Disaster Posts

Most resources in crisis informatics are in English and are annotated at the level of the whole post. A survey of studies from 2020 to 2024 found 91 new corpora, of which 89 include text [@lewis2025tapping]. Of these 89, 47 are in English only, and only 7 of the 91 are annotated with entities, relations, or events. The main datasets for the two tasks of this study are also in English. HumAID provides 77,196 English posts from 19 disasters annotated with humanitarian categories [@alam2021humaid]. HUMAID-NER adds entity annotations to 60,000 of these posts, so the same posts are annotated for both tasks [@ali2026humaidner].

Most Philippine studies of disaster posts trained a model for a single task. @ermino2022urgency classified posts by urgency, @somido2023actionable classified them by informativeness, and @yute2021satellite identified the locations affected by a volcanic eruption. Only one Philippine study identified in this review addresses both classification and extraction. @caoile2025urdaneta did not train a model but queried GPT, a commercial LLM, and evaluated the approach only on simulated comments. Yet smaller pretrained models fine-tuned on annotated data have outperformed LLMs that were given no examples of the task. This result was found in general text classification [@bucher2024finetuned], in the classification of crisis posts [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot], and in Tagalog NER [@miranda2023tlunifiedner].

No dataset identified in this review annotates the same Taglish posts for both humanitarian classification and NER. HUMAID-NER, the only dataset with both annotations on the same posts, is in English [@ali2026humaidner]. @zou2025typhoon trained a single model for both tasks on Chinese typhoon posts, but the place names came from an existing NER dataset, so the same posts were not annotated for both tasks. This gap is part of a wider shortage of resources. Taglish is widespread in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish], yet Filipino lacks many of the datasets, tools, and pretrained models available for English [@cruz2022tagalog]. The existing Tagalog NER datasets are also drawn from news, Wikipedia, historical newspapers, and posts on other topics, not from disaster posts [@miranda2023tlunifiedner; @ramos2023tfnerd; @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner].

## Multi-Task Learning

Multi-task learning trains a single model on several related tasks so that what the model learns from one task helps it learn the others [@caruana1997multitask]. A widely used design is hard parameter sharing, in which the tasks share one encoder and each task keeps its own task head [@vandenhende2022dense; @khanal2021location; @lin2023libmtl]. The tasks that share an encoder need not work on the same unit of text. Humanitarian classification assigns one category to a whole post, and NER makes a prediction for every token [@ali2026humaidner].

Sharing an encoder can also lower computational cost. A multi-task model computes the shared layers once for all tasks, so it needs less memory and produces predictions faster than separate single-task models [@vandenhende2022dense; @lin2023libmtl]. During training, it needs more computation for each update but often less in total than training each task separately [@caruana1997multitask]. Disaster studies have given these savings as a reason to use a multi-task model [@wang2021transformer; @ali2026humaidner] but have not measured them.

However, sharing an encoder can cause negative transfer [@vandenhende2022dense; @royer2023scalarization], and its causes are still debated. The usual explanation concerns the task gradients, the directions in which each task pushes the shared encoder to change during training. The gradients may conflict, so that a change that helps one task harms the other. One gradient may also be much larger than the other and dominate the change [@yu2020pcgrad; @gama2026uniform]. The link between gradient conflict and performance is not direct, however. @royer2023scalarization found that models with many gradient conflicts usually performed poorly, but among models with fewer conflicts, the number of conflicts did not predict performance. Conflicts also became more common toward the end of training, while the loss kept falling.

For NER and classification specifically, @zhu2025prefinetuning traced the conflict to opposite demands on token representations, the numbers that the encoder produces for each token. NER makes entities of the same type more similar, and classification makes the tokens of a text more uniform. In that study, training on both tasks lowered the average NER score over five datasets from 77.1 to 76.4. PCGrad, a multi-task optimizer, raised it only to 76.5. In contrast, adding small modules for each task to the last two layers of the encoder restored it to 77.1.

For disaster posts, training a whole-post task together with a token-level task has produced mixed results. On Chinese typhoon posts, plain multi-task training changed the F1-score from 0.854 to 0.860 for place names and from 0.876 to 0.875 for damage types [@zou2025typhoon]. On English crisis posts, training location identification with three other tasks improved it in most settings, but the results for the other tasks were not reported [@khanal2021location]. On English disaster posts, @ali2026humaidner trained with fixed task weights and observed that classification declined after the third epoch while NER continued to improve. They attributed this pattern to the much larger number of training signals from NER. None of these studies examined Taglish, and none compared more than two multi-task optimizers.

A multi-task optimizer determines how the training signals of the tasks are combined into a single update of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. The simplest optimizers keep the task weights fixed. Equal weighting gives the tasks the same weight [@kurin2022unitary], and linear scalarization uses fixed weights chosen by trying several values [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization]. The remaining optimizers are the SMTOs [@gama2026uniform]. Some of them adjust the task weights during training based on the losses, and the others combine the separate gradients of the tasks [@lin2022rlw; @lin2023libmtl]. @tbl-optimizers lists the 13 optimizers evaluated in this study, which are drawn from seven benchmark studies (Section 3.2).

| Optimizer | Family | How It Balances the Two Tasks |
|:------------------|:-----------|:----------------------------------------|
| Equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with the same weight |
| Linear scalarization [@xin2022mtohelp] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with fixed weights selected through weight sweeps |
| Random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw] | Loss | Draws new task weights at random at every update |
| Uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss | Gives less weight to the task whose predictions are more uncertain |
| DWA [@liu2019mtan] | Loss | Gives more weight to the task whose loss is falling more slowly |
| GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm] | Gradient | Adjusts the task weights so that both tasks learn at a similar speed |
| MGDA [@sener2018mgda] | Gradient | Combines the task gradients into the smallest update that improves both tasks |
| PCGrad [@yu2020pcgrad] | Gradient | When the task gradients conflict, removes the part of each that works against the other |
| GradDrop [@chen2020graddrop] | Gradient | Where the task gradients disagree in sign, keeps one sign chosen at random |
| IMTL [@liu2021imtl] | Loss and gradient | Scales the task gradients so that the update favors neither task, and keeps the losses at a similar size |
| GradVac [@wang2021gradvac] | Gradient | Adjusts the task gradients toward a target similarity tracked during training |
| CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] | Gradient | Finds an update close to the average of the task gradients that most helps the task gaining least |
| Nash-MTL [@navon2022bargaining] | Gradient | Treats the tasks as players that bargain over the shared update |

: Multi-Task Optimizers {#tbl-optimizers tbl-colwidths="[24,14,62]"}

Studies disagree on whether SMTOs outperform fixed task weights. Five comparisons found little or no advantage. @vandenhende2022dense reported that fixed weights chosen by trying a set of values outperformed nearly all the methods that set the weights automatically. Both @xin2022mtohelp and @royer2023scalarization observed that linear scalarization matched or outperformed the SMTOs, and @xin2022mtohelp also found that tuning the training settings mattered more than the choice of optimizer. In the comparison by @kurin2022unitary, equal weighting performed as well as the SMTOs when it was combined with standard techniques from single-task training that keep a model from fitting its training data too closely. In the comparison by @lin2022rlw, random weights performed comparably. These authors proposed random weighting as a baseline that any new optimizer should beat. In contrast, @gama2026uniform found that SMTOs outperformed equal weighting on more complex problems. On two similar tasks, the SMTOs learned weights close to equal and only matched it.

These comparisons used images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text, and none involved disaster posts or Taglish. The optimizers can still be applied to posts in any language, because they act on the losses and gradients and not on the text itself. @xin2022mtohelp, for example, applied the same optimizers to both images and translation. How well they perform, however, depends on the problem [@gama2026uniform].

The optimizers also differ in training cost. Those that combine the gradients of the tasks must compute a separate gradient for each task, which takes additional time and memory. This cost can be reduced by computing the gradients only at the output of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. In @xin2022mtohelp, computing a gradient for each task lowered training speed from about 12 to about 5 updates per second, and in @kurin2022unitary, the SMTOs took longer per epoch than equal weighting. @royer2023scalarization questioned whether removing conflicts at every step justifies the extra computation and memory. Such costs matter because they make deep learning research harder for those with fewer computing resources [@schwartz2020green]. Even so, none of the multi-task disaster studies reviewed here reported training time or memory.

@tbl-matrix compares the key studies reviewed in this chapter with the present study. The rows are in four groups, which are multi-task disaster research, single-task and LLM-based disaster models, a study of NER and classification outside disaster text, and benchmark evaluations of multi-task optimizers.

|:---------|:---------------------|:-----------------------|:------------------|:------------------------|
| @ali2026humaidner | BERT-large and RoBERTa-large shared by two task heads, with fixed task weights or uncertainty weighting | HUMAID-NER, 60,000 English disaster posts | Classification macro-F1, NER micro-F1 | English only, results on validation data from one run, two optimizers, no single-task models of its own, no training time or memory reported |
| @wang2021transformer | BERT and other encoders shared by two task heads, with equal weighting | TREC Incident Streams English crisis posts, 6,658 test posts from 15 events | Information type F1, priority scores, ranking (NDCG), harmonic mean | English only, whole-post tasks only, equal weighting only, no training time or memory reported |
| Khanal and Caragea [-@khanal2021location] | BERT, RoBERTa, or ALBERT shared by four task heads, with equal weighting | A separate English crisis post dataset for each task, with 1,000 training posts each | Location F1 | Only the location task reported, separate datasets for the tasks, equal weighting only, no training time or memory reported |
| @zou2025typhoon | Chinese BERT-base shared by a place-name head and a damage head, with fixed loss weights | 6,000 MSRA NER texts for place names, 6,000 Weibo typhoon posts for damage types | Precision, recall, and F1 for both tasks | Chinese only, tasks trained on different datasets, fixed weights only, no training time or memory reported |
| @alam2021humaid | Support vector machine, random forest, fastText, and transformer classifiers | HumAID, 77,196 English posts from 19 disasters | Weighted precision, recall, and F1 | English only, classification only |
| @ermino2022urgency | Artificial neural network | 4,020 English, Tagalog, and mixed posts about Typhoon Ulysses | Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 | One binary task, 120 validation posts |
| Somido and Reyes [-@somido2023actionable] | Logistic regression on word counts, word weights, and word vectors | 5,000 posts from five Philippine disasters in CrisisLexT26 | Accuracy, precision, recall, area under the curve, F-score | One binary task |
| @yute2021satellite | NER model, support vector machine on satellite images | 18,987 posts about the 2020 Taal eruption, 230 for training, DIWATA-2 images | NER F-score | One volcanic event, locations only |
| Caoile and Aviles [-@caoile2025urdaneta] | OpenAI GPT in an extract, transform, and load pipeline | Simulated Facebook comments for Urdaneta City in Filipino, Ilocano, and Taglish | Accuracy, F1, processing time, user acceptance | Simulated comments only, commercial LLM instead of a trained model |

| @xin2022mtohelp | Linear scalarization compared with MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, IMTL, and random loss weighting | Machine translation, Multi-MNIST, CityScapes, CelebA | Translation quality (BLEU), image task scores, training speed | Translation is the only text task |
| @kurin2022unitary | Equal weighting compared with MGDA, IMTL, PCGrad, GradDrop, and random loss weighting | Multi-MNIST, CelebA, Cityscapes, Meta-World robot tasks | Accuracy, success rate, training time per epoch | Image and robot tasks only |
| @lin2022rlw | Random loss and gradient weighting compared with 12 SMTOs | NYUv2, CityScapes, CelebA, Office-31, Office-Home, paraphrase and part-of-speech tasks in four languages | Task scores, average change against equal weighting | Each text problem is one task in four languages |
| @lin2023libmtl | LibMTL library with 13 optimizers and 8 architectures | NYUv2 | Task scores | Images only |

| Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] | Equal weighting compared with 14 SMTOs | Multi-MNIST, Cityscapes, QM9 molecules | Task scores, average change against single-task models | Images and molecules only |

As @tbl-matrix shows, no prior study evaluates multiple multi-task optimizers and measures training cost on Taglish disaster posts annotated for both tasks.

## Synthesis of Related Literature and Studies

The reviewed studies point to three trends. First, datasets and models for disaster posts have been built mostly from English text, and the Philippine studies either trained a model for one task or relied on a commercial LLM [@lewis2025tapping; @ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @yute2021satellite; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Second, training classification together with a token-level task such as NER has produced mixed results [@zou2025typhoon; @khanal2021location; @ali2026humaidner], and one study traced negative transfer between the two to conflicting demands on the shared encoder [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. Third, studies disagree on whether SMTOs outperform fixed task weights, and their comparisons used images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text, not disaster posts [@vandenhende2022dense; @xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @lin2022rlw; @royer2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform].

These trends leave two gaps. The first is that no dataset identified has the same Taglish posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. The only dataset that has both annotations on the same posts is in English [@ali2026humaidner], and Taglish and Filipino have few annotated resources [@herrera2022tweettaglish; @cruz2022tagalog]. The first and second research questions address this gap. The study therefore builds such a dataset, designs a multi-task model for it, and measures the performance of single-task models on it as the baseline.

The second gap is that none of the studies reviewed compares multi-task optimizers for these two tasks on Taglish posts, in either negative transfer or training cost. None of the multi-task disaster studies compared more than two optimizers or reported training time or memory. Because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], results from other kinds of data cannot settle the choice for these posts. To answer the third research question, the study therefore compares the 13 optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory. To answer the fourth, it compares the final model with the single-task baselines.
